newsitem.title: USA: Long, slow flood cleanup under way in Grand Forks.
newsitem.headline: Long, slow flood cleanup under way in Grand Forks.

text.p: Ruined possessions were piled high along the potholed streets of Grand Forks on Friday as residents tried to scrub away the mess left by floodwaters that have wrecked many lives.
Toilets that actually flushed and working telephones were among the few hopeful signs, although what little fresh water ran through contaminated pipes was undrinkable.

Residents also took heart in the charity of a mysterious benefactor -- the speculation was that the donor was a wealthy California woman, possibly the widow of McDonald's founder Ray Kroc or Madonna -- who pledged earlier this week to give $2,000 to each flood-damaged household. The donation could amount to $10-$15 million.

At least 1,000 homes in Grand Forks were destroyed or damaged beyond repair, federal officials said, along with hundreds more across the Red River in East Grand Forks, Minnesota, as the bloated river spilled over dikes and through streets and homes two weekends ago.

Somehow, more than 50,000 people fled the two cities without the loss of a life, but a subsequent fire in downtown Grand Forks burned unchecked above the floodwaters for two days and laid waste to several businesses.
In an older section of Grand Forks, Bryon Novotny rejoiced as a Coast Guard crew finally drained the hundreds of gallons of stinking fuel oil that had sat in his basement all week.
"I couldn't go in the house," the social services worker said of the oily stench.

In the basement, the clothes washer had floated off its moorings and was sitting at an awkward angle, and the furnace and hot water heater were likely ruined. Mementos that could not be saved in the hurried evacuation two weeks ago were destined for the mound of trash on the curb.
"The story is that nobody thought it was going to be bad as it was. We thought we might get a little water, but not this," Novotny said, who counted himself among the lucky ones.
Downtown Grand Forks remained a virtual ghost town except for the occasional police or National Guard patrol, and some buildings nearer the river remained submerged.
Questions lingered about how forecasters could have underestimated the river's crest, with some blaming the dikes built elsewhere or the damming effect of bridges.

More than 21,000 people have applied for federal emergency assistance and officials were hauling in six-by-30 foot house trailers for the displaced. They were warned the trailers may be home for a year or longer.

Most people made the daily trek to Grand Forks from temporary quarters in nearby towns, although some had flouted a nightly curfew in Grand Forks by covering windows with black plastic. Many families had split up, sending their children to schools elsewhere.
"We want to welcome people back into the community," East Grand Forks Mayor Lynn Stauss said, ending the curfew.

Among other moves made to restore a measure of normalcy, officials announced the return of limited mail service, garbage trucks rumbled down some streets, the hospital emergency ward re-opened and summer school classes were scheduled to begin in two weeks at the University of North Dakota in Grand Forks.
Although swirling floodwaters polluted with raw sewage, fuel and dead livestock had largely receded, the question faced by many residents was whether to rebuild -- and where.

Few people had flood insurance, and most were without work or paychecks. Federal officials said $4 million in emergency aid had been dispensed so far and long-term aid in the form of loans would come later.
Even the $2,000 per household promised by the cities' anonymous benefactor, dubbed the "Angel," was seen as a limited resource given the scope of the losses.
Local officials were considering banning structures in the most flood-prone areas, and Grand Forks' public works director Ken Vein estimated infrastructure damage at $250 million.

Across the flood-stricken region which included North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota, the Federal Reserve estimated $1.75 billion in losses. President Clinton has pledged to provide nearly $1 billion.

The northward-flowing Red River was battering dikes and concrete barriers guarding the Canadian provincial capitol of Winnipeg. Sandbag dikes burst, forcing 240 residents out of two Winnipeg apartment buildings.
About 29,000 residents in Manitoba have been displaced and four Canadians have died so far in the most extensive Red River flooding there since 1852.
